entry.evidence: Separating true signals from false signals remains a challenge.

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text (jats_text), checked against the published PDF

steps.action: The authors pose the problem of telling true reflectors from noise-generated false peaks in ACF-derived reflection responses, and limit the scope to noise in horizontally stratified media.
steps.quote: Separating true signals from false signals remains a challenge.

steps.action: The authors take from prior drilling studies that a sediment-basement velocity discontinuity exists in the study area, which makes the area a known-answer test region.
steps.quote: The existence of this boundary has been confirmed by drilling down to the basement layer at several sites

steps.action: The authors assemble MeSO-net vertical accelerograms (200 Hz) for M>=2 JMA-catalog earthquakes from 2008 to 2021, deeper than 80 km and with incidence angles of 5 degrees or less.
steps.quote: we selected earthquakes at depths greater than 80 km

steps.action: The authors build the error-estimation method: narrow-band whitening, noise-window sigma, 1000 normally distributed noise traces subtracted from the P-window trace, an ACF ensemble mean and SD per event, and an inverse-variance weighted stack with its SD.
steps.quote: Based on this assumption, we obtained 1000 candidates for the earthquake signal

steps.action: The authors take borehole well logs at Hi-net N.SHMH (velocity, density, resistivity, basement at 1.514 km) from earlier studies as the reference two-layer structure for nearby station E.STHM.
steps.quote: The sound velocity and density measured in the well logs indicate that the subsurface can be adequately modeled with a two-layer model.

steps.action: The authors design the test: E.STHM is expected to show a single reflector at 1.5 km and no other significant ones. They add 2D transect profiles with J-SHIS depth conversion and a comparison with the conventional unweighted procedure (§2.3 ¶2).
steps.quote: we applied our method to data from Station E.STHM to test whether the reflector at 1.5 km could be identified

steps.action: The authors compute the 1000-member ACF ensemble, its mean and 3-sigma for the largest (M4.5) event at E.STHM, and find a significant negative peak at a lag of 1.450 s apart from the near-zero-lag artifact.
steps.quote: The amplitudes of the ensemble average are less than or only slightly greater than three times the standard deviation

steps.action: The authors vary the number of random traces (100, 1000, 10,000) and the assumed noise level (2x and 3x) to check the behaviour of the error estimate.
steps.quote: The standard deviations vary little with the number of traces

steps.action: The authors convert the ACFs to reflection responses and depth with the well-log velocity profile, then stack events by weight in decreasing order of magnitude up to 33 events, tracking the amplitude-to-sigma ratio.
steps.quote: The prominence of the positive peak at 1.5 km increases with an increasing number of stacks.

steps.action: The authors compare the stacked significance profile with the borehole-known structure: only the 1.5 km peak is significant below 0.5 km, as expected.
steps.quote: [...] that the peak at 1.5 km is the only significant reflector at depths greater than 0.5 km

steps.action: The authors vary the frequency band (1-5 Hz up to 15-20 Hz) and the earthquake depth limit (60, 80, 100 km; §3 ¶6). The reflector is clear below 10 Hz, the 60 km limit yields false peaks above 3, and the 80 km limit gives the clearest image.
steps.quote: Below 10 Hz, the prominence of the positive peak at 1.5 km is high.

steps.action: The authors apply the method to all stations along the ENE-WSW and ESE-WNW transects and map significance-colored 2D reflection profiles, finding west-dipping and weak east-dipping reflectors.
steps.quote: There are clear west-dipping reflectors from 139° 45′ E (depth: 3 km) to 140° 20′ E (1 km) along the ENE–WSW transect

steps.action: The authors process the same transect data with the conventional unweighted, max-normalized procedure: the same reflectors appear, but among many false peaks.
steps.quote: However, in Fig. 4c, there are many other positive and negative peaks; most of them are deemed false signals

steps.action: The authors test the method on synthetic waveforms (Additional file 1, Text S2), giving detectable reflection coefficients of 0.03 to 0.1 and showing that random noise yields false reflectors below 3 sigma.
steps.quote: The simulation also showed that random noise causes false reflectors with amplitudes less than three times the standard deviation

steps.action: The authors overlay the J-SHIS velocity-layer boundaries on the transect profiles: reflectors are clear where the medium is close to two layers and less prominent where it has three layers.
steps.quote: The reflectors are clearly imaged at the sites where the intermediate (Miura) layer is thin enough to be negligible

steps.action: The authors propose explanations for missing reflectors: an intermediate Miura layer that reduces the impedance contrast, a gradual velocity increase (after Yoshimoto and Takemura 2014), and few earthquakes in the east.
steps.quote: These three-layer or gradually increasing velocity structures are possible explanations for the absence of prominent reflectors

steps.action: The authors check the premise of white Gaussian noise: the noise amplitude distribution is tested against a normal distribution (Fig. 5a,b; Text S4) and the covariance is shown small for lags above 0.075 s (Text S3, Fig. S4).
steps.quote: Our statistical tests showed that the assumption of the normal distribution is not dismissed at 5% significance level

steps.action: The authors derive analytically, decomposing the ACF and invoking the central limit theorem, that the candidate ACFs should be normally distributed, so that 3 sigma corresponds to 99% confidence.
steps.quote: This threshold is consistent with the 99% confidence level if the ACFs obey a normal distribution.

steps.action: The authors compare the empirical distributions of ACF deviations at several lags with the normal distribution for the largest and the smallest events (Fig. 5c,d; Text S4).
steps.quote: The excellent fit between the two distributions and our statistical tests

steps.action: The authors retain the method as giving a quantitative single-station reliability measure for each reflector, with frequency and medium-type limits stated.
steps.quote: The method gives a quantitative measure for the reliability of each reflector from the observations at a single station

end.claim: The noise-subtraction Monte Carlo method yields error estimates for earthquake ACF reflection responses that image the borehole-known sediment-basement discontinuity well above 3 sigma, while peaks at other depths stay below or near 3 sigma, with the signal clear below 10 Hz.

decisive_move.sentence: The comparison of the stacked significance profile at E.STHM with the borehole-known two-layer structure, in which only the 1.5 km peak is significant, is what turns the procedure into a characterized capability.

gates.evidence: Action: the data come from an existing archive, but station E.STHM was chosen because its expected single 1.5 km reflector was known from well logs (§2.3 ¶1). Claim: the method could have failed to raise the 1.5 km peak above 3 sigma, or could have passed false peaks; the 60 km depth limit did produce false peaks above 3 (§3 ¶6). Registration: the expected reflector depth and the 3-sigma threshold were set from prior knowledge, but the 80 km depth limit was judged the clearest after comparing results at this station (§3 ¶6).

imports.item: Monte Carlo simulation of Gaussian noise realizations to propagate noise into ACF uncertainty
Inverse-variance weighted averaging and its standard deviation
Spectral whitening and two-pole zero-phase Butterworth bandpass filter
Central limit theorem to argue that the ACFs are normally distributed

novelty_claims.quote: We present a method to quantify the errors in ACFs and extract true reflectors with high reliability.
Our method realizes an evaluation of the amplitude

limits: No review file or earlier version was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. Additional file 1 (Texts S1-S4, Figs. S1-S4) was not supplied; the synthetic test, normality tests and covariance check are coded from the main-text summaries only. The decisive test is a single station (E.STHM) with known structure, and the same well-log velocity used to define the expected reflector also converts lag to depth. The transect results have no independent ground truth beyond the J-SHIS model. The 80 km earthquake depth limit was chosen after comparing images at the test station (inference: an analysis choice made after seeing the result). The 3-sigma threshold is justified by an assumed normal distribution. Sub-claims: frequency dependence of detectability (clear below 10 Hz) is regularity_in_range; the reflector geometries along the transects and the explanations for missing reflectors (Miura layer, gradual velocity) are best_explanation; detectable reflection coefficients of 0.03-0.1 from synthetics are capability_characterized. Composition: capability_first is the nearest fit, but the walk is method construction followed by a known-answer validation rather than exploration of a new phenomenon.

disagreements.target: Conventional ACF procedure (unweighted stacking, amplitudes normalized to the maximum)
disagreements.support: Fig. 4c shows that the conventional procedure yields many positive and negative peaks deemed false that obscure the reflectors, while the weighted, error-scaled profiles suppress them.
disagreements.quote: In the conventional method, the meaning of the amplitudes of reflection responses from ACFs was unclear.

disagreements.target: Whitening bandwidth used in previous studies (e.g., Oren and Nowack 2017; Chimoto and Yamanaka 2019)
disagreements.support: A narrower 0.0305 Hz bandwidth gives flatter spectra, more consistent with the white-noise assumption the method needs.
disagreements.quote: [...] bandwidth for the whitening (0.0305 Hz) was narrower than that used in previous studies

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Wider bandwidths used in previous studies
alternatives_considered.reason: Flatter spectra, more consistent with independent normally distributed (white) noise samples
none given (the SDs vary little with the number of traces)

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Deeper than 60 km (113 events) or 100 km (20 events)
alternatives_considered.reason: 80 km showed the clearest image; 60 km produced false reflectors, 100 km a weaker peak from fewer stacks

alternatives_considered.chosen: Error-weighted stacking with display scaled by significance
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Conventional procedure without error weighting, normalized to maximum amplitude
alternatives_considered.reason: Highlight reflected signals that are statistically significantly larger than the errors
A trade-off between false and minor reflectors; a high threshold suits poorly studied areas

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Noise designed with the same covariance as the data
alternatives_considered.reason: The covariance is small for lags above 0.075 s, which are the lags interpreted
Ambient noise requires a different approach, left to future studies
